title: Practice Set PMSI2 — Reading the Per-Task Distribution
description: Mid recognition track: read the per-task duration distribution. Distinguish skew shape (one tail) from GC pressure (uniform high) from spill shape (uniform-but-disk). The diagnostic vocabulary that separates a 15-minute debug from a 3-hour one.

datasets.description: Schema reference (sample rows). Mid memory & skew scenarios reference NordGrid at mid production scale (12M meters across 12 regions, 24× the junior dataset).
Substations reference (~200 rows at mid scale). Anchors broadcast-eligibility scenarios.

tasks.title: Skew Shape vs GC Shape vs Spill Shape

description.context: Three NordGrid pipelines have the same wall-clock runtime (~12 min) but three different per-task duration histograms. The senior engineer pastes all three in a Slack thread and asks the team: same runtime, three different shapes, three different fixes. Which is which?
description.task: Which is skew, which is cluster-wide GC, and which is spill?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Task Count Each: 200

Wall Clock Each: ~12 min

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
Histogram A — per-task duration
  Min  P25   P50   P75   Max     Tasks
  2s   2.5s  2.6s  3.0s  12min   200
  Tasks 0-196: 2-3 sec
  Tasks 197-199: 12 min each

Histogram B — per-task duration
  Min     P25     P50     P75     Max     Tasks
  3.2min  3.5min  3.6min  3.8min  4.1min  200
  All 200 tasks: 3-4 min, very tight distribution

Histogram C — per-task duration
  Min  P25   P50   P75   Max   Tasks
  55s  62s   75s   3min  4min  200
  ~150 tasks: 1-2 min
  ~50 tasks: 3-4 min (with elevated spill metrics)

fields.label: Which is skew, which is cluster-wide GC, and which is spill?
options: A is GC pressure (3 outliers stuck in long pauses), B is skew (uniform high duration = same large work per task), C is spill (tight P25-P75 with high max). The diagnostic is the absolute max.
A is spill (3 tasks pushed to disk), B is skew (every task hit the same slow path), C is GC (gradual slowdown from accumulating heap pressure). Sudden vs gradual distinguishes spill vs GC.
A is skew (3 tasks far slower; canonical long-tail). B is cluster-wide GC (uniform high duration). C is spill (elevated mean with moderate max plus elevated spill metrics on slow tasks).
All three show the same problem — slow tasks. Same fix applies to all: enable AQE skew handling, which addresses any tail-heavy distribution by splitting slow partitions automatically.
fields.correctAnswer: A is skew (3 tasks far slower; canonical long-tail). B is cluster-wide GC (uniform high duration). C is spill (elevated mean with moderate max plus elevated spill metrics on slow tasks).
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Inverts the mapping.Long-tail outliers (A) are skew, not GC; uniform duration (B) is cluster pressure, not skew.

tasks.psReference: PSI3 lesson 4 (Data Skew detection), PSI8 lesson 8 (Spill and Disk I/O), PSI9 lesson 4 (Reading Per-Task Distributions).

tasks.title: Per-Task Distribution at 200/200 Tasks Equal — Slow Anyway

description.context: A NordGrid mid-level engineer's pipeline takes 30 minutes when the senior expects 8. The Spark UI Stages page shows 200 tasks all completing in roughly the same time (8.5–9.2 min each, 200/200 evenly distributed). No outliers. No skew. The senior asks: this looks healthy on paper but it is 4× too slow.
description.task: What does the equal-but-slow shape with elevated spill tell you?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Task Count: 200

Executor Count: 4

Executor Memory: 4g each

Expected Runtime: ~8 min

Actual Runtime: 30+ min

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
Stage 4 — groupBy('date') over 12M meter rows

Tasks    Min      P25      P50      P75      Max     Skew?
200      8.5min   8.6min   8.8min   9.0min   9.2min  No (tight, 200/200 equal)

Executors: 4
Executor memory: 4g each
Per-task spill bytes: 1.8 GB average
Spill events per task: 4-6 (avg 5)
Shuffle write per task: 60 MB

Expected stage time: ~8 min
Actual stage time: 30+ min

fields.label: What does the equal-but-slow shape with elevated spill tell you?
options: Hidden skew that the histogram is hiding by showing max but not the long tail. Fix: enable spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled to surface the hidden skew via AQE skew handling.
Uniform spill across all tasks — every task's working set exceeds executor memory, every task spills to disk, disk I/O dominates. Fix: raise --executor-memory OR increase shuffle partitions.
Network bottleneck — the 4 executors saturate cluster bandwidth during shuffle read, so each task waits for shuffle blocks. Fix: enable spark.shuffle.compress=true to reduce on-the-wire bytes.
The pipeline is healthy and 30 min is correct for 12M rows on 4 executors; the 8 min expectation is unrealistic. Fix the SLA in team docs, not the code.
fields.correctAnswer: Uniform spill across all tasks — every task's working set exceeds executor memory, every task spills to disk, disk I/O dominates. Fix: raise --executor-memory OR increase shuffle partitions.
fields.rationale: 8 GB average spill and 5 spill events per task — the spill metrics are the smoking gun.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents 'hidden skew' that the data contradicts.200/200 equal duration rules out skew.
Option C: Misreads spill bytes as network bytes.

tasks.psReference: PSI8 lesson 8 (Spill and Disk I/O), PSI9 lesson 4 (Reading Per-Task Distributions).
